[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

IN THIS ISSUE…

Research in neuropsychoanalysis is helping to understand how brain structures are affected by psychological processes in early infancy, laying down the biological substrate of the human unconscious. Allan Schore reports evidence supporting the idea that mother-infant interactions directly influence the organization of brain systems in the early critical period of growth, and how these systems can be reorganized in the adult as a result of psychotherapeutic experiences.

Metaphor's special role in psychotherapy is due to its claims on the imagination, traditionally believed to provide a direct route to the unconscious. Terri Eynon investigates new theories in cognitive linguistics that show language to be fundamentally structured by metaphor, underpinning and extending the psychoanalytic view that metaphor is at the heart of language and meaning.

Symbol formation, the most remarkable achievement of the human mind, is discussed by Giovanna Rita DiCeglie. Patients produce, unconsciously, symbolic representations that enable the analyst to understand the people, thoughts and feelings within the patient's internal world.

In the past year or so there has been a worrying reduction in the number of submissions of clinical articles to the British Journal of Psychotherapy. If we are to continue to learn from each other and increase our body of knowledge, we must have the freedom to report our clinical experiences, questions, nagging doubts and mistakes in publications, as well as in public forums. It is generally agreed that without case reports we would be immeasurably impoverished. There can be no development in the field by means of theory alone: as Freud put it, theoretical argument yields no fruit and we must turn to the clinical material on which we rely.

Since we hold as a first principle the protection of our patients, I suspect, to a certain degree, it is the fear surrounding confidentiality and the consequences of its breach that inhibits writing up clinical material. The issue of confidentiality in journal articles is now being discussed widely in the field, with suggestions of a number of acceptable ways that case studies can be made anonymous and debate regarding the wisdom or otherwise of asking patients for their permission to publish excerpts from their therapies. Please email for more information.

An Interrupted Life: The Diaries and Letters of Etty Hillesum 1941-43 by Etty Hillesum, with a preface by Eva Hoffman and introduction by Jan G. Gaarlandt; translated from the Dutch by Arnold J. Pomerans. Persephone Book No. 5. Published by Persephone Books, London, 1999; 430 pages; £10.00.

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone

London Centre for Psychotherapy, London

Jennifer Silverstone  

Persephone Books are beautiful objects, soft backs in dove grey without adornment save the lovely endpapers, which come with a matching bookmark. In this Diary they were ‘taken from “C.S.P., a Bauhaus fabric designed for the De Ploeg Company, The Netherlands, in 1932-35 by Otti Berger d. Auschwitz 1944”’. This endpaper - a print of fabric - is perhaps, Etty's bedspread’, so they say in the Persephone Catalogue No. 1. The Bauhaus designer's beautiful pink and blue drawn thread-work wore out long ago with time and use, perhaps, and more likely, the fabric had a longer, fuller, though inanimate life than those who constellated around it; for the designer, the weaver, and countless nameless others and Etty herself all perished.

For it is ‘Etty’ that she so quickly becomes, familiar and friendly, a confiding voice, beloved, full of hope and promise, and the reader, or at least this reader, develops an attachment to what is not just her life, as she describes it being lived, but the life force, the almost palpable instinctual drive to stay alive. We long for her to survive to continue the journey that is so full of promise, and almost suspend belief in the inevitable ending.

Whilst musing about life and its vicissitudes one has to encounter death, for this is what this life brings so poignantly and prematurely with it. Here I take issue with that lower case ‘d.’ which marks the premature end of Otti Berger's life on the frontispiece and the solemn reference on the end piece ‘Etty Hillesum died in Auschwitz on 30th November 1943’. Death comes naturally, linguistically, albeit more frequently than premature illness and accident take account of. But death did not come to Auschwitz and visit Etty Hillesum: she perished, was gassed or murdered but she did not die. Death is ‘the fact or act of dying, the end of life, the final cessation of the vital functions of an individual’ (OED). To use the word diminishes the trauma of a snatched ending, killing requires a battle, a murder requires an other. To perish is to ‘to pass away entirely, to come to nothing, to be lost or destroyed. To come to a violent sudden untimely end. To suffer destruction, to lose life, to cease to exist’ (OED). Etty Hillesum perished, as did all the other victims of the Holocaust. She left Westerbork, on the outskirts of Amsterdam in Wagon No. 12 on 7 September 1943. She dropped her last note from that transport and it was picked up by a farmer and postmarked 15 September. She perished on 30 November 1943. She was 29 years old.

Introduction: Glimpses of a Life

Jenny Rycroft

Jenny Rycroft

2 Modbury Gardens, London NW5 3QE. [email: jenny.pearson-rycroft@virgin.net]

Jenny Rycroft  

I feel very privileged to be introducing this conference. When I saw the list of speakers I wondered what I could add to the day. Then I reflected that, having shared 20 years of his life and listened to many stories of the years when I was not around, it might be of interest if I were to set the scene with an impression of Charles, the man I knew, and describe the rather surprising background from which he emerged to become a psychoanalyst and writer of the post-Freudian era - one who, according to his obituary in The New York Times, ‘offered a generation of therapists new ways to interpret not just dreams but Freud's entire legacy’.

Before I begin my story I want to say how very sad I was to hear that Anthony Storr had died in March. He was one of Charles's closest friends and their conversations ranged widely - a very free exchange between two independent thinkers in the traditions of Jung and Freud respectively. So, as well as a sense of personal loss at Anthony's death, I feel a keen disappointment that he is not speaking here today. Some of us who heard him speak at the memorial meeting the family held at Burgh House in Hampstead, in November 1998, remember the depth and clarity of the account he gave then of Charles's ideas and, especially, his writing, ranging from his classic 1960 paper ‘Beyond the reality principle’ to his ‘hilarious’ account of Communism at Cambridge in the 1930s. Anthony said:

I enormously admired him as a writer. Analysts are not always noted for the clarity of their writing! Think of Lacan! But Charles's writings are crystal clear. He was rightly uneasy about Freud's ambivalent attitude to phantasy and many of his best writings are concerned with the positive aspects of the creative imagination which he refuses to dismiss as escapist as Freud tends to do.

A one-time Communist who wrote humorously about Communism, a Freudian who wrote about the primacy of the imagination, Charles was always original, paradoxical and surprising.

Journal of Analytical Psychology46, 257-273, 2001

His Mother-Tongue: From Stuttering to Separation, a Case History

Margaret Wilkinson

This paper delineates the transference and countertransference experiences in the analysis of a patient whose presenting symptom and main concern was his stutter. I suggest that oral-sadistic rather than anal-sadistic hostile elements may be identified in this patient's particular stutter, I focus on its significance in terms of object relationship: my patient's struggle to ‘get born’, to emerge as a separate other. I argue that early symbiotic fusion needs in conflict with the need to separate produce his stutter. Speech and language are seen as the vehicle for separation and the stutter as a flight from separateness back to an illusion of fusion with mother.



Journal of Analytical Psychology46, 325-334, 2001

The Future of Analysis

Coline Covington

The aim of analysis is to enable our patients to differentiate themselves from their past. The question we face as analysts is whether we are in fact neurotically bound to repeat the past. This paper addresses this question by considering some of the reasons that there is a ‘crisis in analysis’. Two central problems within the practice of analysis are identified as contributing to this ‘crisis’: (1) a view of the patient as ‘enemy’, or as innately destructive; and (2) a trend towards here-and-now interpretations within the transference which disregards history and the role of external reality. The danger of such an approach is that it does not allow patients to separate from their hateful primal scenes and to become free of neurotic guilt. When we are anxious about our own destructiveness and aggression and do not link this to a failure to form a loving relation, we run the risk of fostering compliance and conformity within our patients and within our own professional societies. In contrast, it is the recognition of the past and its influence on the present that makes analysis a tool for evolution.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

[BJP@jarundale.demon.co.uk]

Jean Arundale  

In This Issue …

Esther Bick's contribution to psychoanalysis is uncontested, in particular her theorizing on the notion of the skin as a container for unintegratable infantile psychic contents, on ‘adhesive identification’ as a defence, and her pioneering development of infant observation at the Tavistock Clinic. Her unpublished Membership Paper was read to the British Psychoanalytical Society in 1948. It describes the analysis of an acutely anxious woman with multiple disabling symptoms. Roger Willoughby, who discovered the paper in archives, introduces the work.

Pre-symbolic, chaotic individuals respond to the relational mode when interpretations are felt to be intolerable. Marguerite Valentine writes of how the self evolves in the treatment of regressed and borderline patients.

The victims of racial violence suffer a profound attack on their identity, precipitating often-catastrophic infantile anxieties and breakdown. Narendra Keval reports on a patient victimized by his own violent father.

Patients with physical disorder are not usually treated with psychotherapy. In an MRC-funded experimental trial with Irritable Bowel Syndrome patients, Stephanie Howlett and Else Guthrie report the benefit of farewell letters in enhancing the effect of positive change.

A pilot study for the treatment of Borderline and other Serious Personality Disorders carried out in the NHS by The Edinburgh Project is reported by Alison Cookson and her colleagues. The results of short-term (one year, once weekly) psychoanalytic psychotherapy measured improvements in impulsivity, acting out and other symptoms in this difficult to treat group of patients.

Borderline patients benefit from the structure and containment of the NHS day hospital. Jean White and her colleagues write of the long term treatment of seriously disturbed patients along psychodynamic lines by the therapeutic team.

The American psychoanalyst Stephen A. Mitchell inspired many British psychotherapists working within the relational tradition. Bernice Laschingera and Kate White offer an Appreciation of his life and work.

Relating in Psychotherapy: The Application of a New Theory by John Birtchnell. Published by Praeger, London, 1999; xiii & 269 pages £D49.95 hardback.

Dale Mathers

Dale Mathers

Dale Mathers  

Theory is an explanation, an exposition of the abstract principles within a science or art, an idea which has not yet been proved - conjecture. To be ‘new’ - like New Labour? - freshly grown or lately discovered. What remains to be discovered by psychotherapists about relating? We've had premodern, modern and postmodern approaches; psychoanalysis, analytical psychology and humanistic therapies which all value competing ‘theories’ - usually venerated statements of sage founders and elder states persons. The same is true of the ‘Joseph's Technicolour Dreamcoat’ of ‘New Age’ therapies. What can be said that is new? Something simple.

Science proceeds, spiral-fashion, from theory to observation and observation to new theory by hypothesis generation and falsification. The main elements of relating can be imagined on two axes - love and will - or, in the new terminology, (distant and close), (upper and lower). On each axis, relating can be positive and negative. This concept is central (pp. 12-13). Positive relating is what we should all strive for and negative relating falls short of this ideal. A versatile person (who relates positively) could score equally on each axis. Therapy of relating is a matter of accentuating positive and minimizing negative. How Humans Relate (Birtchnell 1993) outlined research on relating and derived a mathematical model, a task possible for someone fluent in many theoretical languages: scientific precision, artistic creativity and years of hands-on clinical experience.

John Birtchnell, whose fluent English makes this book easy to read, uses languages from medicine (trained at Edinburgh), research (he worked for the Medical Research Council for many years), and vocabulary from psychology, psychiatry and art therapy. He has drawn on considerable experience to narrate a theory of relationships, illustrated with lively clinical examples. He also introduces a new research tool, the Persons Relating to Others Questionnaire (PROQ).

The book is a distillation, I think, rather than ‘new theory’. Concepts basic both to object relations theory and analytical psychology are reconstrued throughout. (Distant and close) partly corresponds to a Gestalt therapist's concept, (‘top dog - under dog’), (upper and lower) partly to old-fashioned ideas about ‘class’. For example, (distant and close) (upper and lower) could describe relations between any two internal objects (ego-states, archetypes or subpersonalities); the delicate intimacy between father, mother and infant in a family or oedipal triangle; between (Self and ego), (Self and other); between social and cultural groups.

Ann Casement

Ann Casement  

Brief Background to the Draft Psychotherapy Bill

The eight bodies that have been meeting at the House of Lords since the autumn of 1999 to work together on the draft Psychotherapy Bill are the Association of Child Psychotherapists; Association of Psychoanalytical Psychotherapists in the NHS; British Confederation of Psychotherapists; British Psycho-Analytical Society; British Psychological Society; Royal College of Psychiatrists; Tavistock Clinic; United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy. These eight bodies were identified by the Department of Health as the key stakeholders in the field of psychotherapy.

Meeting at the House of Lords on 16 June 2000

Initial Responses to the Draft Psychotherapy Bill

Lord Alderdice reported on the responses he had received to date following First Reading on 18 May 2000 of the draft Psychotherapy Bill. He reaffirmed his undertaking that the Bill would not proceed to Second Reading without the support of the stakeholders group.

Prior to the publication of the Bill, Lord Alderdice had held a briefing with approximately 100 MPs and Peers who are known to have an interest in mental health issues. A great deal of support for the Bill was expressed on this occasion and a number of meetings will take place in the near future between Lord Alderdice and government ministers. The campaign group, Mental Aftercare Association (MACA), have also welcomed the Bill.

Representatives from the Association of Child Psychotherapists had recently held a meeting with representatives of the Department of Health about other matters and the Bill had been discussed there. They were told that the Minister of Health wished to make a statement regarding the Bill.

The British Psychological Society (BPS) brought to the attention of the meeting that they had recently been told that their Order in Council to regulate psychologists under the new Health Act of June 1999, one which empowers the Government to call for the regulation of professional organizations, would not be likely to occur until 2002. In view of this, the BPS have asked that the Psychotherapy Bill should not be brought sooner than 2002 in order to enable the Bill to contain an opt-out clause for psychologists.

The Uninvited Guest: Emerging from Narcissism towards Marriage by James Fisher. Published by Karnac Books, London, 1999; 299 pages; £26.95.

Helen Robinson

Helen Robinson

Member, British Psycho-Analytical Society, London

Helen Robinson  

It might at first appear as something of an oddity that the figure of ‘the uninvited guest’, upon which my reading of James Fisher's impressive text will concentrate, is the imagination. I think it is not usual in psychoanalytic work, clinical or theoretical, for the practitioner to ascribe his findings to the work of his or her imagination. It has, of course, been acceptable to attribute findings to work that is derived from conscious and unconscious sources. But, from Freud onwards, it might be said that it would have been positively catastrophic for any psychoanalyst to examine carefully the contribution of the imagination to the production of his thinking, his findings, his writing.

And yet it is in this sense that I see one of the many meanings that the phrase ‘the uninvited guest’ has here and in other contexts, that is, the unacknowledged and unexamined presence in the Mind and in the mind of all psychoanalytic thinkers from Freud onwards, of the imaginative powers. Charles Rycroft, an exponent of the imagination in his thinking and writing, became an absent, perhaps uninvited and unwanted guest at the psychoanalytic feast as the years progressed, precisely because he argued, in Margaret Arden's words, ‘that unconscious imaginative processes underlie the development and maintenance of a sense of reality just as much as they do neuroses’ (Arden 2000). Rycroft does have an entry on ‘Imagination’ in his A Critical Dictionary of Psychoanalysis, a little and famous work that has spawned innumerable others. This entry lies alongside the more readily used psychoanalytic term, fantasy/phantasy (conscious and unconscious) which we familiarly use to direct ourselves to the internal world. Rycroft writes of the imagination as ‘the process or faculty of conceiving representations of objects, events, etc., not actually present’ (as does the OED). He distinguishes the process of the imagination as producing ‘results which are either (a) imaginary, in the sense of being fictitious, unreal, etc., or (b) imaginative, in the sense of providing solutions to problems which have never previously been so solved, or in the arts, creating artefacts which nonetheless reflect or enhance experience’.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis82, 431-447, 2001

Psychoanalysis and Cognitive Behaviour Therapy - Rival Paradigms or Common Ground?

Jane Milton

The author suggests that contemporary enthusiasm for cognitive-behavioural therapy reflects our longing for swift, rational help for psychological suffering. Competition for funding threatens the psychoanalytic presence in the public sector. The psychoanalytic and cognitive-behavioural models are contrasted, and the relative richness of the psychoanalytic paradigm outlined. The author suggests that a cognitive model is commonsensical, but less complex, with less potential explanatory and therapeutic power. She discusses how the analytic stance is always under pressure to ‘collapse’ into simpler modes, one of which resembles a cognitive one. This also occurs inevitably, she argues, when attempts are made to ‘integrate’ the two models. Cognitive and ‘integrated’ treatments nevertheless have the advantage that they are less intrusive and hence more acceptable to some patients. Selected empirical process and outcome research on cognitive and psychoanalytic therapies are discussed. Brief psychotherapies of either variety have a similar, modestly good outcome, and there is some evidence that this may be based more on ‘dynamic’ than ‘cognitive’ elements of treatment. Formal outcome studies of more typical psychoanalytic psychotherapy and of psychoanalysis itself begin to suggest that these long and complex treatments are effective in the more comprehensive ways predicted by the model.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis82, 533-543, 2001

Mapping the Landscape: Levels of Transference Interpretation

Priscilla Roth

The author argues that there are distinctly different kinds of transference interpretation, each of which might be valid in particular circumstances in analysis, but which contain and imply different understandings of what is meant by a ‘transference interpretation’. She suggests that transference interpretations may be at any one of four different levels, and she describes these levels as ranging from interpretations that point to links between current events in the analysis and events from the patient's history, through interpretations that link events in the patient's external life to the patient's often unconscious phantasies about the analyst and the analysis, to interpretations that focus on the use of the analyst and the analytic situation to enact unconscious phantasy configurations, sometimes pulling the analyst into the enactment. Material from four consecutive sessions of an analysis is presented to illustrate how all levels of transference interpretation may be part of a lively and meaningful analysis, but how the level of interpretation may change as the level of understanding deepens within a session and from one session to the next.

This paper will provide theoretical and clinical evidence for the significance of relating to and dissociating from the object in the development of a regulatory function. A selective review examines psychoanalytic views concerning the interactive nature of innate and environmental factors in development. The role of trauma is also considered as a contributing factor in individual differences. Relevant clinical material is described from two sessions in the treatment of a traumatized young woman with bulimia, focusing on the regulatory function in the therapeutic relationship. The patient frequently dissociated from the therapist as object and substituted the resulting loss of regulation with a pendulous movement between over-indulgence and deprivation. This created significant implications for treatment. The clinical findings suggest that the inclusion of these different aspects may be necessary factors in understanding the developmental pathway from intolerable frustration/impulsivity to an internal sense of containment.

London

John Southgate  

In this guide to memory and illusion Phil Mollon manages the difficult task of detailing scientific and clinical research whilst giving clear summaries and checklists that are useful for psychotherapists. There are many clinical examples, some drawn from his own experience and others - psychoanalytic, psychological and physiological sources including reports and cases - drawn from both historical and new material.

In addition, the book is very readable and most sides of the debate in this complex area of work are examined. It is also a useful source of contemporary research from many different sciences. The themes in this book include: trauma and false memory, implicit and explicit memory and neuropsychological factors; multiple personality dissociative disorder; repression, implicit memory and dissociation; experience of remembering and PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder); hypnosis; Freud and recovered memories (very good summaries of Freud's classic cases: psychotherapy students could be advised to buy this book for this section alone); hypnosis and drugs; true and false narratives in psychoanalysis; evil, cults and ritual abuse; guidelines, summaries and lessons of the debate; and general principles of treatment and management.

There is far too much material in this book to cover extensively in a review. I have chosen, therefore, to concentrate upon the subject of repression and dissociation because this is an important issue for many psychotherapists. Mollon summarizes the complexity of this issue:

Differences between dissociation and repression

Dissociation involves an alteration in consciousness; repression does not.

Dissociation involves splitting of consciousness, whereas repression involves splitting of the mind.

Dissociation is directly observable, either by the patient or the therapist; repression is inferred.

Dissociation evolves commonly, but not exclusively, in response to exogenous trauma, whereas repression applies more commonly to internal conflicts.

Playing with Reality: III. The Persistence of Dual Psychic Reality in Borderline Patients

Peter Fonagy and Mary Target

This paper is a contribution towards understanding the difficulties of severely borderline patients as they are uncovered within the psychoanalytic process. The authors aim to extend a model from previous papers, bringing a developmental perspective to bear on self-representation and self-organization. This model rests on an understanding of the child's experience of psychic reality in both normal and neurotic people. The authors explore the relevance of these developmental ideas in thinking about severe borderline and related disturbances seen in adult patients, from the point of view of both understanding the pathology and considering technique. Illustrations are given from a case that helped to prompt the formulation of these states in terms of persistent, pervasive distortions of the experience of psychic reality. There is then an attempt to elucidate the difficulties of borderline patients in tolerating both separation and intimacy, consideration of the way in which bodily experiences may be used as an equivalent of mental experience or contact, and a discussion of the impact of disturbances in the experience of psychic reality on the analytic process.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis81, 875-892, 2000

Becoming a Subject: Some Theoretical and Clinical Issues

Roger Kennedy

The author presents a cluster of theoretical and clinical thoughts and some clinical material concerned with the issue of subjectivity in psychoanalysis. For convenience, he has organized these thoughts around the notion of ‘beoming a subject’. This entails a process of recovery, or discovery, of unconscious subjective elements. There is a discussion of what we mean by the term ‘subject’, with reference to various strands of philosophical and psychoanalytical thinking. It is suggested that becoming a subject involves a shift towards a ‘subjective position’. This refers to how being a subject involves some capacity to take up different positions without becoming fixed in any frozen state of being. In order to be fully in touch with another person, in a truly subjective position, one begins to grasp the other's point of view; the other is seen as other, as a person or a subject, in a context, orientated to others and being affected by others. A subjective position involves allowing experiences of the other to interpenetrate oneself, so that they make an impact. In order to clarify these ideas, clinical material from the analysis of a bulimic patient is presented to illustrate some of the difficulties for this patient in becoming a subject and allowing the analyst to make an impact on her.

Kate Springford and George Craig

George Craig

George Craig  

Although the book is not called, nor even subtitled, ‘Essays in honour of Hanna Segal’, it might as well be; indeed Otto Kernberg, in his Foreword, actually presents it as ‘the second of two books in honour of Hanna Segal’ (the first being Reason and Passion, also edited by David Bell). In the event, respect for Hanna Segal is just about the only thing the essays have in common, in spite of the editorial efforts of David Bell, who contributes a sizeable (22-page) Introduction, as well as an essay on Dennis Potter's The Singing Detective. The book is organized under two headings: ‘Art and Literature’ (four essays); and ‘Mind and Society’ (six). In the first group, apart from Bell on Potter, there are essays by Ronald Britton on Rilke (The Duino Elegies), Igněs Sodré on Flaubert (Madame Bovary), and John Steiner on Sophocles (Oedipus Rex). The larger section has Michael Rustin on ‘Psychoanalysis: the last modernism’; Richard Wollheim on ‘Emotion and the malformation of emotion’; Michael Feldman on ‘Pride’; Léon and Rebecca Grinberg: ‘Psychoanalytic perspectives on migration’; Pearl King on the analysis of old people (‘In the end is my beginning’ - words attributed to T.S. Eliot, although he actually wrote ‘In my end is my beginning’, even more appropriate); and A.A. Mason: ‘A psychoanalyst's look at a hypnotist: a study of folie à deux’.

Although the reviewer, faced with such variety, is obliged to offer in fairness a comment on each of the essays, some general remarks are possible and, indeed, as will soon be clear, essential. The first concerns the section ‘Art and Literature’. Whenever psychoanalysis is applied to a literary work, it is important to ask how far it illuminates the work (literature is, after all, not a body of ready-made evidence or case material). For the essays offered here, the answer varies between ‘hardly at all’ and ‘a great deal’. Igněs Sodré's account of Madame Bovary (‘Death by daydreaming’) has valuable things to say about daydreaming, but is disappointing in its approach to Flaubert.

Uneasy Triangles: A Brief Overview of the History of Homosexuality

Anne Zachary

Anne Zachary

8 Fitzjohn's Avenue, London NW3 5NA. [email: zacweeks@aol.com

Anne Zachary  

In the past, homosexuality has been classified as a sin, then as a crime, then as an illness. It sat uneasily between these three, passionately argued away from each in turn throughout recent history. But as time moves on into a new millennium, homosexuality has never quite left the negative environs of these unsatisfactory categories, or of the strong emotions, shame, disgust and anger, as explored in David Jones's paper.

In thinking about this it occurs to me that there are many aspects of the debate and also other related issues which coexist in similarly uneasy triangular relationships. Any of these can quickly become polarized into a two-dimensional conflict. My talk in Oxford set out simply to list examples in a free associative way in an attempt to keep the discussion from setting fast into a polarization on any one side of any one of the triangles. This polarity might be concerned with diagnosis: perversion, inversion, ‘normality’ (neurosis); or with groups of people: the Church, women, homosexuals; or with mechanisms: paranoia, prejudice, persecution. What emerged in the discussion was the suggestion that another triangle could be completed from topics I had presented two-dimensionally by concentrating only on sexual practice and object choice. From the floor it was pointed out that I had left out the concept of gender identity. It was further clarified that, historically, the concept of gender developed only in the 1960s.

History in general is not strictly what we think it was. We add to it our own retrospective view in the light of further developments. It is surprising that the term, ‘homosexuality’, was first coined as recently as 1869 by Benkert. This led to the labelling of homosexuals, defined by their sexuality rather than this being assigned a proper place within their whole personality.

A version of this paper was given as an introduction to a conference workshop in which David Jones presented his clinical paper, also printed in this issue, at the EFPP Millennium Conference, ‘Changing Times, Changing Relationships’, Oxford, 7-9 April 2000.

Any thoughtful reading of Beyond the Pleasure Principle amply confirms David Black's conclusion: the properties of the death drive as postulated by Freud in 1922 bear no relationship to the drive theory of psychoanalysis because, as David Black notes with admirable economy, ‘The return of organic matter to the inorganic state does not make a demand on the mind for work; it happens reliably with or without the mind's participation’. Similarly David Black points out the difficulties with an indirect route to the death drive originating in Freud's earlier neuroscientific training as expressed in ‘A project for a scientific psychology’, which to my mind, in disagreement with David Black, is a minefield rather than a seed-bed of ideas. And one is relieved to find that he quite rightly rejects what he calls indirect affective roads to the death drive which reduce Freud's motivation to his feelings at the time - World War I, the dangers to his sons Martin and Ernst, his weariness with life or, even and intriguingly, his feelings about the loss of Jung just before World War II. When coupled to his analysis of the subsequent development of the death drive as a metaphor for human destructiveness rather than as a biological reality, I think we are in a position to recognize with him that the death drive was in fact a detour.

We should stop teaching the death drive in our trainings. And we should recognize, with David Black, that the death drive was a detour of historical interest, but is no longer of real psychoanalytic interest. Ilan Diamant  

The impact of trauma on the narrative memory or self-experience of victims of childhood sexual abuse and the current controversy about the status of recovered memories of abuse, are addressed in this paper. I will particularly focus on one form of knowing psychic trauma, that is, the subjective experience that is organized under transference and the countertransference phenomena.

Let me start with a short account of a session with Miss I, a 26-year-old patient, whom I see three times a week. Miss I started the session, noting that she could not sleep throughout the previous nights. She then described her experience as a trainee teacher. She said that the pupils did not have the book from which she had planned to work on so she had to improvise. She told them two short stories, ‘Ugly Duckling’ and ‘The Disguised Egg’. Her tutor criticized her. She felt confused. She felt she wanted to give her tutor much credit for what she was but, at the same time, she was frightened that the tutor would control her.

Her associations went on to describe many sleepless nights, lying next to her exboyfriend, whom she had described as continually controlling and sexually abusing her. She recalled her physical feelings. She was restless. Her joints were aching. She said: ‘It was like rheumatic pain in my muscles… It felt cold, the feeling engulfed throughout my body’. At the same time as she spoke about it she gently stroked her arms and thighs. She said that the feelings she described were signs of negligence. She added that she wouldn't like anybody to lie in bed next to her and that she needed some vitamins to feel more balanced.

She moved on and talked about her father. She said that, when she was a child, he was quite tender. He would sit next to her bed, gently stroking her arms and thighs with his big palm. He would sit and tell her pleasant and relaxing stories.

Throughout that session she spoke in an emotionally detached way. For me it felt strikingly real. I found myself articulating a narrative. It was as if I listened to a story evoked by the stress associated to her recent sleepless night. The story depicted a teenager who was sexually abused by her boyfriend, recalling images of herself being a sleepless girl caught in ambivalent feelings towards controlling figures who caressed and infuriated her.

[[RunningHead]]

The Development of Charles Rycroft's Thought

Margaret Arden

Margaret Arden

50 Highlands Heath, Putney, London SW15 3TX. [email: ardenml@waitrose.com]

Margaret Arden  

Charles Rycroft began his private practice in 1947, before completing his psychoanalytic training. He was still practising a week before his death in 1998, just over half a century later. I shall try to give some idea of the development of his thinking from his early writing, when he was within the mainstream of the British Society, to his late development as an independent thinker and writer. I shall be using two sources of information - his own published work and my personal recollections of him. Rycroft was my training analyst until 1962 and I read all his papers soon after they were published. I had always been in the habit of thinking for myself and he never made any attempt to influence me. Through reading his work I was able to continue on my own path. I had a second analysis with him many years later during which I began to write papers of my own. He always made it clear to me which of my ideas he accepted and where he disagreed with me. He never made any value judgments about what I wrote but always made me feel that I had his support in my exploration of ideas. He approved in general of the way in which I built on his work in my own writing, but sometimes thought I was trying to describe things which he felt were better left unsaid. From the early 1980s we met as fellow members of the 1952 Club, where psychoanalytical ideas are discussed in a non-political atmosphere.

I shall begin with a brief account of his background and education. Rycroft was born in 1914 and spent his early years in the secure environment of an upper-class country house. His mother was the second wife of Sir Richard Rycroft, the 5th Baronet, whom Charles described as the most important man in the village. His father died when Charles was 11 and his mother had to return with her four children to her own family, as her stepson inherited the title. The death of his father and his mother's subsequent depression greatly affected Charles's future. His father had expected Charles to have an army career. This was also the expectation at his school, Wellington College, which had been founded for the sons of officers killed in the First World War.

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Barnstaple, Devon EX31 4JB. [email: j.a.holmes@btinternet.com]

Jeremy Holmes  

To write about one's analyst, even after an interval of more than 20 years, is far from straightforward. The pitfalls of idealization, denigration, sibling rivalry, collusion and narcissistic identification all mitigate against objectivity. On the other hand, to have been in a position to test a particular analytic approach in vivo must count for something, and being a patient can stimulate curiosity and a fascination with the analyst's ideas which, with the passage of time, may reflect mature internalization that goes beyond acting out or oedipal intrusion. But if I stray outside the bounds of balanced exposition, perhaps due allowances will be made.

My paper falls into three parts. Firstly, I summarize Rycroft's critique of psychoanalysis as he encountered it in the period 1940-1960 while training and working within the British Psycho-Analytical Society. Secondly, I try to elaborate the theoretical perspective and psychotherapeutic methods which he developed in opposition to the conventional psychoanalysis of his day. Thirdly, I link these ideas to themes in contemporary psychoanalytic psychotherapy, in an attempt to show how many of his ideas have passed into common currency, and thus, without forming a distinct school or movement or acquiring overt followers, he has significantly contributed to the Zeitgeist.

First, I must say something about Rycroft's style. Le style c'est l'homme certainly applies to him in both his literary and therapeutic personas. The ‘Real’ Therapist

Dear Editor

Could I use your correspondence column to put forward a view on a point Dr Bateman raises in his interesting article, ‘Integration in psychotherapy: an evolving reality in personality disorder’ (BJP 17(2): 147-156).

In discussing what seems to help, he says, ‘The active ingredient is the tripping up of the unconscious, being faced with the unexpected, and seeing things in a new light’ (p. 153). I see that as part of an understanding of what is happening in terms of what is going on within the patient, but I wonder if there may be more to it if one thinks in terms of something that is happening between the therapist and the patient. I have been gradually coming to suspect that one of the things patients look for is what might be called the ‘real’ therapist, by which I mean the person the therapist actually is, as opposed to the ‘professional’ person the therapist has been taught by their training to be.

To explain the point in more detail: when Dr Bateman wonders if it is the surprise of the therapist doing something different, i.e. a cognitive therapist using interpretation or a therapist who uses a transference focus using a cognitive intervention, that helps, I would agree. But I think it is not just that the ‘unconscious is tripped up’. I think the surprise is that the therapist lays aside their normal ‘professional’ way of working and uses an intervention that comes from the ‘real’ person of the therapist. The idea is similar to that put forward by Symington in his paper ‘The analyst's act of freedom as agent of therapeutic change’ in The British School of Psychoanalysis: The Independent Tradition edited by Gregorio Kohon (1986), and I have come across similar examples from other therapists and in my own work.

I am not for one moment suggesting that technique should be set aside. But I do think that patients are continually interested in who this person really is that they find themselves in therapy with, and that meeting the ‘real’ person can, at times, help. What I have not yet formulated are any views on when and how it is appropriate to reveal the ‘real’ person. I am also aware that, as most of the communication that takes place between two people is thought to be unconscious, the patient may unconsciously be aware of who we really are all the time!

The Edinburgh Project: A Pilot Study for the Psychotherapeutic Treatment of Borderline and other Severe Personality Disorders

Alison Cookson , Jonathan Espie and Kathleen Yates

Kathleen Yates

Claremont House, Off Framlington Place, Newcastle upon Tyne NE2 4AA

Kathleen Yates  

Patients with borderline and other severe personality disorders take up a disproportionate amount of time from psychiatric, accident and emergency and community services. The Edinburgh Project was commissioned to examine the process and outcome of time-limited psychoanalytic psychotherapy with these patients. The project provided once weekly psychotherapy over the period of a year for 19 patients and administered a range of psychometric self-report questionnaires at the beginning of the therapy, monthly and at 3, 13 and 20 months post-therapy. This article presents the findings of those studies and relates them to the psychotherapeutic process. The results suggest that the model adopted in Edinburgh can help to reduce symptoms, acting out, impulsive feelings and behaviours and that these reductions are maintained at post-treatment follow-ups.

Individuation as the Adaptive Response to Mental Pain

Nina Vasilyeva

Nina Vasilyeva

Russia. [email: anvi2@online.ru]

Nina Vasilyeva  

This paper tries to show that Joseph Sandler's concept of individuation is applicable to the current situation in Russia on the level of the individual, the family and society. Examples are given to illustrate this thesis.

Life in harsh conditions such as those in Russia today may create an illusion that it is the environment which is to be blamed for the unhappy state of being. This is the most common reaction among Russian people to the present situation where people live through hard times. This brings the examination of different individual reactions to the painful situations into focus.

No doubt crisis situations may exist as external sources of pain in their own right. On the other hand, it is obvious that some individuals can deal with the painful state that arises only by reapplying past solutions, while others may be able to adapt to the new situation. This statement contributes to common analytic experience that crisis demands are significant to the extent to which they are involved in the individual's inner conflicts. What may appear as an external crisis may be predominantly an internal one.

To gain an understanding of this process we may use the psychoanalytic model formulated by Joseph Sandler (Sandler 1989). He considered individuation to be the most adaptive response, from the point of view of the ego. Individuation is a process that involves ‘working through’ in a manner analogous to mourning. It involves the adaptive abandoning of lost ideal states and their replacement by new ideals that are both ego and reality syntonic. In contrast to those who saw the individuation processes as occurring in a specific developmental phase, Sandler considered individuation to be a line of development that continues throughout life and, in particular, is associated with typical developmentally and culturally determined tasks and crises. Sandler saw the danger of individuation not in terms of threats of object loss (as did M. Mahler), but stressed the painful necessity for the child to give up ideal states of the self previously experienced.

Metaphor: The Impossible Translation?

Terri Eynon

Terri Eynon

61 Melbourne Street, Coalville, Leics LE67 3QU. [email: alderoak@ntlworld.com]

Terri Eynon  

The linguistic concept ‘metaphor’ has an established place in clinical as well as theoretical psychotherapy. It has been seen as analogous to or even fundamental to the analytic concept of transference. Metaphors have been thought to have a special role in enhancing therapist-patient communications. By contrast, in linguistics itself, metaphor has been relatively neglected, viewed as irrelevant and unscientific. That conventional approach to metaphor has recently been challenged by Contemporary Metaphor Theory.

This new theory suggests that language depends upon a largely unconscious system of conventional metaphor. Our bodily experiences are the basis of our understanding of abstract concepts such as emotions and relationships. Novel and imaginative metaphors build upon this fundamental biological structure.

The traditional approach placed metaphor, along with rhetoric and, by inference, psychodynamic thinking, at the periphery of science. Cognitive linguistic research is now showing that language is fundamentally structured by metaphorical processes, which enhances the scientific status of psychoanalysis and supports and extends the view of metaphor as at the heart of language and meaning.

What Remains of Oedipus? Part Objects beyond the Pleasure Principle

Guy Undrill

Guy Undrill

Bristol BS 16 2EW. [email: guy.undrill@bris.ac.uk]

Guy Undrill  

Lacan's understanding of the death drive as an effect of the symbolic chain raises the possibility of a symbolic death (connoting narrative ending) before the subject's biological death. The dying Oedipus in Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus might be thought of as occupying such a position. Lacan asks us to consider what, when his life has completely passed over into destiny, remains of Oedipus?

Nietzsche's ‘untimely meditations’ invite, anticipate and sanction future textual interpretations that Nietzsche himself could not have predicted; similar textual strategies exist in the work of Beckett. Such strategies offer an approach to overcoming the impossibility of adequately narrating a life. The psychoanalytic concept ‘part object’ can be extended to model the way parallel processes are at work in psychoanalysis. Beckett's own retelling of the Oedipus story is considered to show how it attempts to answer the question ‘what remains of Oedipus?’

This paper responds to the BJP editor's call for responses to the journal's symposium on statutory registration by offering a critical analysis of two previously neglected aspects of professionalization: the rapid ‘postgraduatization’ of psychotherapy, and the legitimacy or otherwise of the way in which state regulation is being pursued. The Future of Psychoanalysis edited by Johannes Cremerius. Published by Open Gate Press, London, 1999; 153 pages; £12.99.

Yvette Wiener

Yvette Wiener

London

Yvette Wiener  

This well-timed collection of essays addresses very actual and pressing preoccupations in the psychoanalytical world. At the time of my reading it, a congress whose title - ‘Call for a States General of Psychoanalysis’ - suggests the urgency of the situation, was taking place in Paris (July 2000) and was heralded by six long articles in Le Monde (6 to 11 July 2000). Meanwhile, in London, a group of psychoanalysts met to discuss links between Freudian theory and neuroscience.

From a variety of backgrounds, Johannes Cremerius and his seven co-writers attempt an exacting analysis of the reasons behind the apparent decline of psychoanalysis and its lack of relevance to the modern world, but also offer possible solutions and a brave invitation to think afresh and to change.

Cremerius, whose essay gave the book its title, notes that all attempts to recognize the crisis and identify its causes have looked for answers outside institutional psychoanalysis. He refers specifically to an edition of The Psychoanalytic Quarterly (1988) and enumerates its findings:

increase in alternative forms of therapy

switch in psychiatry to an approach rooted in biology and behavioural therapy

greater trust in pharmacological forms of therapy

disappointment with the curative effect of psychoanalysis exacerbated by the criticisms of a malevolent press.

Bravely, Cremerius reverses the diagnosis and sees the facts enumerated above not as the causes but as the results of problems and failures within the profession. From the beginning, he underlines the dichotomy between the principles of psychoanalysis, namely liberation through enlightenment, and the spirit of the psychoanalytic movements reflected in the hierarchical and authoritarian structure of the International Psychoanalytic Association from the time of its foundation in Nuremberg; in 1910.

Hysteria by Christopher Bollas. Published by Routledge, London, 2000; 179 pages; £16. 99 paperback.

Ruth Berkowitz

Ruth Berkowitz

London

Ruth Berkowitz  

In his introduction to the book, Bollas lets the reader know that the text will follow what he calls ‘criss-crossing continua’ (p. 2). He describes his task as providing a theory which weaves the famous traits of hysteria into the hysteric form. Weave is perhaps the crucial word because the theory, both of the influences contributing to the emergence of the hysteric and the nature of hysteria, follows an intricate path of interlacing threads through the chapters. The book is based on lectures given by Bollas and he has to some extent stuck to that format. The impetus for the lectures came out of clinical supervisions in the United States and the cases which were presented were ‘clearly hysterics but the majority of the presenters thought of them as borderline personalities’ (p. 2). He goes on to say:

Although in the past, supervisees had certainly presented a variety of character disorders, by the mid-1980s almost every case presented was hysteric. What was I to make of this? Gradually, it seemed to me to be an unconscious demand in the therapeutic community to reconsider hysteria. Disenchantment with the over-embracing concept of the borderline diagnosis was clear, and thinking the hysteric through the theoretical lenses of the borderline personality had become something of a tragedy. (p. 2)

The theory, he says, is fundamentally Freudian, although he at times disagrees with Freud. Other influences are the British Object Relations school (Winnicott and Klein), Lacan and, importantly, the patients from whom he has learned about hysteria.

The first chapter called ‘The Characters of Analysis’ describes the object relation, in particular to the primary object which distinguishes the narcissist, the borderline, the schizoid, the pervert and the hysteric. The hysteric differs from the others in that they witness (my italics) intense, but detached, maternal love of the self.

Tyrannical Omnipotence in the Archetypal Father

Warren Colman

This paper sets the archetypal relationship between the tyrannical, devouring father and his sons in the context of a disjunction in the parental couple (syzygy) whereby the role of the maternal feminine is eclipsed and excluded. This is shown to originate in an omnipotent defence against infantile dependence on the mother. Successful liberation from the father's tyranny requires the restoration of mutuality between the internal couple. Although the main focus is on the internal world (and a detailed clinical illustration is given, showing the working out of this process in the analytical relationship), reference is also made to political tyranny, attitudes to the control of Nature by technological means and patriarchal forms of masculinity. The Chronos myth is amplified through the use of two modern variants in the films The Terminator and Star Wars.

‘Stream of Consciousness’ and ‘Ownership of Thought’ in Indigenous People in Central Australia

Leon Petchkovsky

Fifteen Central Australian Aboriginal adults (8 patients, 7 colleagues) were presented with a culturally modified version of Flavell's ‘stream of consciousness’ experiment (pictures of persons with empty or ‘busy’ thought-bubbles, and an invitation to assign a picture to the mental state of a second experimenter seen reading or sitting quietly). Only 4 people assigned the empty thought bubble to the quiet experimenter. This result was at least as good as that of a sample of Stanford College students tested by Flavell. The experiment provoked detailed comments from the informants about subjectivity, suggesting great subtlety of phenomenological awareness in Central Australian Aboriginal people, and attributing a kind of subjectivity to non-human entities, including inanimate elements. We learnt that the Western Deserts dialect term watiya was reserved for the subjectivity attributed to trees and rocks. The ownership of all thought was attributed to the tjukurpa (the Aboriginal dreaming). These Aboriginal cultural attributions were compared and contrasted with reflections developed by Jung and the postJungian David Holt on the nature of subjectivity, and religious notions of the redemption of matter.

Christina Blackwell and Esti Rimmer-Yehudai

Esti Rimmer-Yehudai

Cramlington, Northumberland NE23 1AX

Northumberland NE61 2NU

Esti Rimmer-Yehudai  

Teaching junior doctors psychotherapy is a difficult task. This paper charts the progress of clinical psychologists setting out on this task, initially finding it impossible, but thinking and working together to develop creative, working groups in which the junior doctors and group leaders learned and developed.

We detail how we run the teaching groups and what it is like to be a member of such a group. We consider the costs and benefits of clinical psychologists teaching junior doctors and the differing cultures of psychiatry, psychology and psychotherapy. We discuss institutional and group defences which create obstacles to learning. We propose a training model based on maternal containment as opposed to pseudo-paternal identifications. Containment of anxiety appears to be necessary for the creation and maintenance of a safe space for junior doctors to learn about psychotherapy.

Peter Hildebrand

London

Peter Hildebrand  

When reviewing this book, I have to declare an interest. My parents sent me to a preparatory boarding school in Brighton from the age of 6 to 12. Had Hitler not invaded France in 1940, I am sure I would have spent my adolescence at boarding school. I have often thought that one of the few good deeds that Hitler ever committed was to frighten my parents into sending me to the United States in 1940, and thus enable me to escape from the boarding school where I had been immured for the last six years.

Looking back nearly 60 years later, I can clearly recognize that the opportunity to live in a warm, loving and supportive environment in an American High School, to mix naturally with boys and girls of my own age and to be free of school uniform, unnecessary rules, fagging and bullying changed my life out of all recognition.

So, when I came to read The Making of Them which examines the British attitude to children and the boarding school system, I found myself in doubly familiar territory. All psychotherapists working in this country meet time and again the inhibited, schizoid English man or woman whose capacity to make enduring close relationships with others has been irretrievably damaged by their experiences at boarding school. For some of these patients, psychotherapy offers a long-sought opportunity to explore and develop their capacity for caring and intimate relations. For others, it represents a tremendous threat to their internal equilibrium, for they have clearly identified with the aggressor and feel terribly threatened when the therapist invites them to express their feelings. I well remember one patient who, when his sister was dying of pancreatic cancer, told me that under no circumstances would or could he allow himself to disclose to me or to others close to him any hint of his very real grief for the fate that had overtaken her.

Historically, these attitudes are of comparatively recent origin: in the late eighteenth century it was a mark of good breeding in gentlemen to be able to break into tears at every opportunity and thus to demonstrate one's sensibility. The public schools were set up to provide cadres for the emerging Victorian Empire: when a young man was sent away to India to administer the affairs of a million or so people, he might well feel that he did not wish to expose his feelings to others particularly, the conquered, and perhaps ‘let down the side’.

Tessa Adams  

To review these publications is to review the series. Clearly Postmodern Encounters as a catch-all concept for a series of mere 70 page publications can seem to be quite questionable, not least by the fact that the publishers have interpreted postmodernism so loosely. This form of publication, which bids to introduce complex theory within such limits that a popularist pocket-book demands, inevitably forces the writer to forfeit exposition at times when it is most needed. The question becomes, at whom are these publications aimed? Is it for university students, trainee psychotherapists or established professionals who are concerned to sift through the complexities of postmodernity? It is difficult to judge, for the level of these essays varies from rudimentary generality that typifies Heaton's introduction to Wittgenstein, to complex critical analysis that Wright affords her postfeminist focus on Lacan. This spread of interpretation could indicate that the authors have a particular catchment group in mind and have appropriately ‘played to the gallery’.

Moving on to discuss each essay in some detail, as indicated above, it is my view that, of the three titles, Elizabeth Wright's Lacan and Postfeminism is clearly the most developed exegesis. This is hardly suprising since her wellknown critical dictionary Feminism and Psychoanalysis (1992) certainly demonstrates her propensity for concise textual analysis.

In many ways Wright's essay is a tour de force. Her critical academic approach means that the argument is systematically set out with a glossary of key terms designed to ensure that all her propositions can be closely followed. Opening with a historical account of the problematic of postfeminism and its relationship to psychoanalysis Wright situates an intensive analysis of Lacan's formulaic account of sexuation.

Else Guthrie

15 Northumberland Road, Sheffield S10 2TT. [email: s.j.howlett@sheffield.ac.uk]

Else Guthrie  

Irritable bowel syndrome patients being treated by brief psychodynamic-interpersonal therapy were given a farewell letter written by the therapist in the final session. The context was a randomized controlled trial to assess the cost-effectiveness of psychotherapy and antidepressant treatment for painful functional bowel disorders. A year after the end of treatment patients completed a questionnaire to evaluate their perceptions of the usefulness of farewell letters. Five case vignettes illustrate different ways in which patients reacted to the farewell letters during and after treatment. Patients who benefited from therapy found the letter helpful as a means of sharing their experiences with others, continuing the work of therapy and dealing with the ending. The letter seemed to act as an embodiment of the therapist or transitional object, facilitating the continued assimilation of problematic experiences. Where therapeutic outcome was poor there was less evidence of helpfulness. Preliminary impressions suggest that farewell letters may be a helpful tool enhancing the benefits of brief therapy.

This volume, a festschrift presented to H. Sydney Klein, comprises some 14 chapters written by his analysands, supervisees, colleagues and friends. In her brief introduction Joan Symington states that the book focuses on the multi-faceted nature of imprisoned pain, and its analytic transformation into pain which can be experienced and therefore worked with.

In the first chapter Anne Alvarez writes that it is still painful for her to read her notes on her first four years of work with 10-year-old Richard. He had become less psychotic but preoccupied with sadistic phantasies in relation to small animals, and had begun to act on them. Other colleagues and supervisors had suggested that this was not unusual for a previously psychotic child. But, when she went to Sydney Klein for supervision, he showed her how her patient was feeling attacked by some of her interpretations. This enabled her to understand that Richard's sadistic behaviour was based on identification with a persecutor. She modified her technique, and Richard ‘began to soften very quickly’ (p. 7). In the ensuing work, Richard became ‘far more collected and together and civilised’ (p. 7). It seems clear that Sydney Klein enabled his supervisee to be in touch with both her patient's and her own pain. This freed the therapist to do better clincal work. It also facilitated her on a journey of engaging with and absorbing the developing literature on projective identification and of evolving her own conceptualization of the ‘grammar’ of projective communications. She elaborates some of her ideas within her chapter. It is no surprise then to also be told that Sydney Klein, though trained as a Kleinian analyst, carved out an independent position within that school, and is also noted for his encouragement of attempts to think independently.

What of the rest of the book? Each chapter includes the author's own clinical material. They vary in focus, range and style. For example, Kate Barrows, in Chapter 5 relates her understanding of Seamus Deane's novel Reading in the Dark to her analytic work with Miss Y. In both cases the inhibition against having a life of one's own is linked to the internalization of ghosts in the family. As a clinician she strives for a careful balance between attending to her patient's conscious thoughts about her shadowy internal objects and her own destructiveness. There is a good outcome. The relationship of her work to her internalized analyst is made explicit by her reference to Sydney Klein's ‘combination of common sense, of intuition and down-to-earth realism’ (p. 79).

Hysteria

Dear Editor

The Spring issue of the journal (17(3)) featured reviews of two recent books on hysteria: Hysteria, by Christopher Bollas, and Mad Men and Medusas: Reclaiming Hysteria and the Effects of Sibling Relations on the Human Condition, by Juliet Mitchell. Both books argue for a wider category of contemporary phenomena that could be regarded as hysterical. Whilst each text is thought-provoking, challenging and illuminating in various respects, there is a potential scientific and professional problem inherent in a loose use of the diagnosis of hysteria.

For example, Bollas refers as follows to another recent book on the subject:

Indeed, as Elaine Showalter (1997) has argued in her brilliant book Hystories, hysteria is alive and well in the form of attention-deficit disorder, chronic-fatigue disorder, alien-abduction movements and the like. (p. 178)

Elaine Showalter is a professor of English who writes about psychiatry, film, theatre and television (according to the note in her book). As such she is not required to adhere to the same standards of scientific and professional care that apply to clinicians who see patients or who write about clinical matters. In that respect, it does not matter that her book is polemical rather than a sober examination of what is currently known about various conditions that may or may not, in any particular case, contain a hysterical element. However, for the clinician faced with an actual patient it has enormous implications if it is assumed that a presenting symptom is hysterical without consideration of a variety of other diagnostic possibilities.

Showalter refers to ‘six psychogenic syndromes of the 1990s: chronic fatigue, Gulf War syndrome, multiple personality disorder, recovered memory of sexual abuse, satanic ritual abuse, and alien abduction’ (p. 12, italics added). There is extensive literature about each of these complex and controversial subjects. Showalter lumps them all together and calls them ‘hysteria’. On what basis can she claim to know that Gulf War syndrome, or chronic fatigue, are ‘psychogenic’? Whilst I cannot claim to be an expert on Gulf War syndrome, I am aware that there are people who are seriously ill with physical and cognitive symptoms that do not correspond to PTSD, and who suspect this relates in some way to having participated in the Gulf War (see National Gulf Veterans and Families Association: www.leiva.freeserve.co.uk/gulfveterans.htm). A number of serious and plausible hypotheses have been proposed, including the possibility of exposure to toxins of various kinds. Similar cautions apply to Bollas's implied assertion that attention-deficit disorder is a form of hysteria. There is a great deal of scientific material concerning ADHD, the current consensus being that the constellation of impulsivity and distractibility results from an inefficiency in the frontal lobes of the brain.

IN THIS ISSUE …

There is a market for brief dynamic therapy and many are engaged in its practice without there being a reliable, systematic model upon which to draw. Ilana Laor contributes to the conceptualization of a brief therapy model and offers a case study.

Freud's death instinct, which he linked with the compulsion to repeat, has been treated with scepticism and rejection in many quarters, yet many analysts find the notion clinically useful beyond simply the metaphorical. This Journal invited David M. Black to reflect upon and to review the concept, and he argues that the death drive was a detour in psychoanalytic thinking, theoretically inconsistent with drive theory, and of historical interest only. Joseph Schwartz responds with agreement, putting forward other ways of thinking about human destructiveness and violence. We will invite further response to this debate in future issues.

Earl Hopper writes a systematic study of hope within the context of contemporary object relations theory and of life's vicissitudes, ultimately defining hope as imagination in the face of trauma.

The theme of hope and hopelessness is further explored by Diana Menzies in her work with an analytic group. She proposes that hope can grow if there is a sharing of true self experiences.

At the BJP/Freud Museum joint conference on The Legacy of Charles Rycroft, the life and work of this exceptional psychoanalyst and psychotherapist were celebrated. Rycroft was for many years the writer who conveyed psychoanalytic ideas to the general public, writing for The Observer, TLS, The NY Review of Books, etc.; thus he was for many years one of the most widely known people in the field. We present the conference papers herein.

Jenny Rycroft speaks of memories of their time together. Margaret Arden and Jeremy Holmes, who were analysands, examine the development of his ideas and their experiences of his technique. Paul Roazen writes of the significance of one of Rycroft's key concepts, ‘ablation of the parental images’ in relation to the history of psychoanalysis as well as the individual. Susan Budd, who was inspired by his writing before training as a psychoanalyst, regrets his departure from the British Society. She examines Rycroft's work from the insider/outsider perspectives.

Although it is a pleasure for me to try to pay tribute to Charles's originality within psychoanalysis, it is, of course, sad that he could not be present to listen to the kind of heartfelt tributes that he fully deserved to hear while still alive. I knew him from 1965 until 1998, and I would guess that he was shy enough not to have appreciated his success as an independent thinker. We fell into a pattern of usually seeing each other at dinner whenever I happened to come over to London, but I have checked my files and there are also approximately 80 letters from Charles. On one of our last evenings together, he did remark that he felt his career as an analyst had been ‘ruined’ by the respective power of two women, Melanie Klein and Anna Freud. It is no doubt true that Charles's reputation and standing temporarily suffered from the complex politics of British psychoanalysis then, when ideological contests made it difficult for independent-minded people to win recognition. Although his A Critical Dictionary of Psychoanalysis1 has become influential and sold well, a book like The Innocence of Dreams,2 even though admired by someone like Graham Greene, did not do as well in terms of sales as one might expect.

At the same time I think that it would be understandable if Charles underestimated his own achievement; even though books of essays and reviews3 cannot be expected to do well commercially, his work was, if only because of the impact of his publishing in The New York Review of Books, capable of being widely influential. Charles was like other early psychoanalytic pioneers in being broadly well educated and cultured. It seems to me that, in the face of the transitory fads and bureaucratic lethargy that afflict all fields, Charles did succeed in being a distinctive and original voice. Even though we no longer have the personal pleasure of Charles's intellect and person, I find there is no problem in bringing to mind some of his most characteristic ways of thinking.

Psychoanalysis has had its distinctive manner of proceeding, and British analysts worked out their own special ways of conceptualizing things.

Susan Budd

Susan Budd

The Provost's Lodging, Queens Lane, Oxford OX1 4AW

Susan Budd  

I should say at the start that I have found it very difficult to write this paper. I have admired Dr Rycroft's writings for many years, but when I came to consider what his legacy to the psychoanalytic world has been and, therefore, what his place in that world had been and might have been, I had the sensation of stepping from a firm rock onto shifting sands. Partly, he had left the British Psychoanalytical Society before I began to train and, partly, the intellectual hegemony that he had reacted against was by that time in some disarray. So I have no personal recollection of him in the Society to guide me, and the landmarks by which he steered are not all recognizable to me. I knew Charles Rycroft hardly at all; I only began to meet him at the very end of his life. In that sense, I am an outsider to those at the Conference who did know him well, either as a friend or in that very odd and special way in which patients come to know their analysts.

The legacy of a psychoanalyst can have several aspects. For most analysts, their most important memorial is their work with their patients, and with their supervisees, if they have them. They may also be active members of their professional bodies, they may also work elsewhere, for example, in the National Health Service, and they may write, either for insiders, i.e. their fellow professionals, or for the general public. Some may write for both. It is for his writings that Dr Rycroft will be chiefly remembered - his writings, and for the fact that he resigned from the British Society but continued to work as a psychoanalyst. This affected the nature of his legacy in several ways.

After his resignation, his analysands could not formally become psychoanalysts. (This, incidentally, is an important hidden cost to the Society of the resignations of senior figures.) He chose to work in private practice, so that his work with analysands remains for the most part hidden and unknown. As Margaret Arden said, after he left the Society very few of his papers described his clinical work in any detail, and so we have no knowledge as to how his views influenced his technique other than by hearing from his analysands. His influence and ideas were exerted through his writing, rather than through holding any organizational posts.

Universities are engaged in a fight for survival, a fact that cannot be doubted by anyone who has ever cast an eye over the supplements advertising places available through the UCAS clearing scheme that appear in the newspapers as soon as the Alevel results are published. The rapid expansion of university courses in the last 10 years, combined with the recent cuts in funding available to students, means that there is intense competition to attract and retain students. There is an increasing awareness that many students arrive at university with difficulties that threaten their chances of academic success. This has forced new thinking on the level and type of support they need, in a context of ever-increasing pressure on the resources available for this.

Ravi Rana's book, published this year, is the latest contribution to a growing literature on counselling students in higher education. This book is part of a series entitled Basic Texts in Counselling and Psychotherapy and the author has combined an explanation of the psychodynamics affecting adolescents and the way in which these are played out in the university setting with a guide to theoretical concepts.

In the first five chapters, the author explains the psychoanalytic concepts that inform her work - she is a psychoanalytic psychotherapist as well as a student counsellor of many years standing - and writes about the developmental stages that adolescents have to negotiate before they can leave home and achieve success in their own right, away from their families. This is an ambitious project. Ravi Rana makes use of a large number of case vignettes - and, though they are illustrative and clearly drawn on extensive experience, this reader felt rather overwhelmed, particularly in the first two chapters. Dr Rana explains they are composite illustrative examples rather than actual students, and they clearly have a vivid presence in her mind.

Mapping a Detour: Why did Freud Speak of a Death Drive?1

David Black

David Black

30 Cholmley Gardens, London NW6 1AG. [email: dmblack@clara.co.uk]

David Black  

When Freud first put forward his relatively late hypothesis of a death drive, he did so using a rather surprising argument from evolution. However, he came to support it with a neuroanatomical argument dating back to the earliest days of psychoanalysis. In this paper I look at these two streams of argument in some detail, and conclude that neither is persuasive. My thesis is then in two parts: firstly that the death drive, as such, probably merits no future in psychoanalytic thinking; secondly that, though mistaken, Freud's discussion of the death drive was hugely productive for the future development of psychoanalysis. Perhaps the abiding interest of the ‘death drive’ lies in this apparent paradox that mistaken theory can be truly fruitful.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

IN THIS ISSUE …

Narcissism, with its distortions of self-esteem, continues to be a central problem in psychotherapeutic work. Jan Ole Røvik describes changes in the superiority/inferiority dimension within a selfpsychological framework, allowing dependence on the object and depressive affect.

A new therapeutic tool that assists the ‘digestion’ of emotional experience is presented by Phil Mollon. Consistent with psychoanalytic and neurological principles, Accelerated Information Processing (EMDR) helps to work through anxiety and trauma.

Cultural influences infiltrate the early transference and countertransference as shown by Antonio Suman and Antonino Brignone. Culturally preformed fantasies in the initial sessions, if uninterpreted, can block the development of the therapeutic relationship.

Francis Grier writes of therapy with three couples who shun sexual relations, showing how oedipal fixations, rigid defences and fear of change can conspire to prevent psychic development and marital satisfaction.

Changes have taken place in the psychoanalytic treatment of homosexual patients. Anne Zachary summarizes the history of our views of homosexuality, and David Jones explores the therapist's strong affective countertransference responses within the context of bisexuality and homosexual object choice.

Literature offers up fascinating examples of personality types. Bernardine Bishop studies Shakespeare's characters, Lear and Prospero, comparing the projecting personality of Lear - blaming, raging - with Prospero's introjecting mode - forgiveness, acceptance and the capacity to love.

John Wright, winner of the Student Essay Prize, writes of the vicissitudes of relating and dissociating as found in work with a young bulimic woman.

Dynamic psychotherapy as taught to junior doctors training in psychiatry, with all the inherent difficulties, is reported by Christina Blackwell and Esti Rimmer-Yehudai who are clinical psychologists in the NHS.

Martin Stanton responds to Jackie Gerrard's critique of Michael Balint, followed by Gerrard's ‘right to reply’.

Bernardine Bishop

Bernardine Bishop

7 Patshull Road, London NW5 2JX

Bernardine Bishop  

My thesis is that King Lear and The Tempest, seen together, offer a map of the trajectory of psychic process from the projective to the introjective mode. Lear remains psychically unseparate, both from his daughters, who constitute a split maternal object, and from kingship, with which he is in projective identification. The Tempest, six years later, takes up and reworks to their resolution the same themes. Prospero learns to separate from Miranda, forgives his enemies, and relinquishes the rewards that come from narcissistic pseudo-potency, in his case afforded by magic powers.
