Mannie Sher  

Transference

This clinical vignette illustrates very well the challenges all psychoanalytical psychotherapists face - when and how to address transference phenomena, particularly during assessment stages and early sessions of treatment. This is never an easy task when either too much emphasis or too little increases the probability of losing the patient. There are particular elements that need to be considered in assessment and early sessions - the patient's pain that brings them to the therapist in the first instance, their expectations of the encounter, often based on previous experiences with a therapist, as in this case, the particular personality structure that could result in the therapist being kept at an emotional distance, or allowed to get close to emotional states.

On reading the material, I felt that the therapist's doubts and vicissitudes of feeling coming through very clearly. My own countertransference, which I had to check constantly, was to push the therapist to get a move on; that she was taking too long to comment on core complexes which a sharply pointed interpretation could have unblocked. I was reminded of the strictures of my supervisor, Pierre Turquet, that, despite psychoanalytical psychotherapy being essentially an analysis of the negative transference, one needs to be cautious in the application of this principle. After all, the patient comes into treatment often for reasons that are not immediately apparent, reasons that he cannot articulate and for which he is seeking a benevolent caring figure to help him access the hidden and the unconscious.

We learn that the patient had two assessment interviews followed by a two-week Easter break and that, to date, he has had nine once-weekly psychotherapy sessions. We also hear that he had had two previous experiences of counselling/psychotherapy; one for two sessions, the other for six. His assessment of these experiences do not instil confidence that he will ‘stick’ this time. Yet, he is now in session 9, pointing to increased chances that he will stay with the current therapist.

Shame, Disgust, Anger and Revenge: Homosexuality and Countertransference

David Jones

David Jones

Grendon Prison, Grendon Underwood, Bucks HP18 OTL [email: davidjones@iname.com]

David Jones  

Homosexuality has a central place in the history and development of psychoanalysis. Freud correctly identified ‘difference’ as a starting place for an investigation into the dynamics of sexuality. Unwittingly he also instigated thinking that raised, among some analysts, a desire for curative action. The absence of insights from the countertransference debate influenced psychoanalytic thinking for a period, obscured the benefits that might accrue from the analyst's recognition of his intrinsic bisexuality and, more recently, fuelled a popular reaction which argues that homosexuality is not a matter for psychoanalytic investigation but a healthy extension of the personality. The profession similarly has been divided. This paper contends that homosexuality should remain an area for psychoanalytic consideration. There are transference and countertransference issues to examine that include shame, disgust, anger and revenge.

While such emotions and reactions are not unique to the area of homosexuality they may lead to particularly destructive effects if left unobserved in our work and in ourselves.

Sue Gerhardt

Flat I, 4 Crick Road, Oxford OX2 6QJ

Sue Gerhardt  

This paper situates a case history in the context of an emerging theoretical perspective, influenced by attachment research, that gives increasing weight to early real interactions. It suggests that the developing individual often has little choice in the kind of relational strategies that their early interactions unconsciously set up. The case history explores how this might have been the case for Marian, and asks to what extent such a patient can subsequently choose to modify her way of relating to others, as an act of selfcreation. It suggests that to a large extent this is determined by her current social context and the vicissitudes of a jointly created therapeutic relationship.

Earl Hopper

Earl Hopper  

Introduction

The title of my article is ‘On the Nature of Hope’. ‘On’ involves an eighteenth-century English conceit. It implies that the phenomenon is really too big and too complex for any one author, and, therefore, that he is allowed to be selective. ‘Nature’ implies, somewhat ironically, that the phenomenon does not belong to religion or magic, but to a realm or domain that permits rational, systematic and sceptical study. Thus my title implies that, in my opinion, the phenomenon of hope is finite and contingent, and is a matter for science, to include the psychological and the social sciences. However, I am certain that Hamlet was right when he admonished Horatio that ‘There are more things in heaven and earth … than are dreamt of in your philosophy’ (Shakespeare, Hamlet, I. iii. 166).

After a brief indication of the scope of the topic, I will define ‘hope’ as it is ordinarily used in English. I will then make several conceptual distinctions that are necessary in order to discuss hope and its vicissitudes. My third task will be to define hope from my own point of view, which is that ultimately hope refers to the ability and willingness to exercise the transcendent imagination within the context of the traumatogenic process. I will focus on the development and maintenance of this human virtue within the context of life trajectories constrained by social, cultural and political factors. Finally, I will discuss some aspects of my view of hope in clinical work. I will not provide a systematic review of the literature, but in future publications I will trace the emergence of my understanding of hope in the context of the development of contemporary object relations theory, and illustrate my argument with clinical vignettes from my practice as a psychoanalyst and group analyst.1

In this paper I investigate some of the problems faced by the couple and the clinician when the presenting problem is that the couple does not have sex. This symptom normally expresses multiple meanings. I restrict myself to exploring the defences against the pain that ensues from unconsciously facing the primal scene aspect of the Oedipus situation, and how the prospect of dismantling these defences feels catastrophic to certain couples. The Dove That Returns, the Dove That Vanishes: Paradox and Creativity in Psychoanalysis by Michael Parsons. Published by Routledge, London, 2000; 226 pages.

Michael Eigen

Michael Eigen

New York

Michael Eigen  

This good work seems to me part of a wider genre which seeks to give dual or multiple tendencies in human nature their due. It seeks at once to acknowledge and heal damage done by over-emphasizing critical analysis at the expense of imaginative intuition or vice versa. I think of an old book, Poetic Diction by Owen Barfield (1964), which shows the interplay of critical and intuitive capacities in poetry. In a way, Parsons does something similar for psychoanalysis.

There are wars in psychoanalysis not just between schools but between sensibilities. Some emphasize psychoanalysis as science, some as art, and there can be spiteful acrimony. Winnicott speaks for a democracy of voices and notes, for example, the difficulty that logical verbalizers and visual or auditory hallucinators have with one another (Winnicott 1989, p. 155). Parsons shows how damaging it can be to exclude precious capacities and how valuable it is to acknowledge their appearance in others. How we relate to who we are not plays an important role in discovering who we are. Often we find bits of who or what we did not become in those around us. In a way, we are carriers of lost or unborn aspects of one another, echoes of inner as well as outer diversity. Together we extend what we cannot live out alone.

Parsons asks what really matters in an analysis and shows that this can take many forms. He begins his book's journey by calling attention to Marion Milner's ‘answering activity’. Before Milner became an analyst in the technical sense, she discovered what she called an ‘answering activity’ in herself, a kind of I-yet-not-I or other in one's being, producing creative moments, the most precious moments of the day. Too often this ‘answering activity’ gets lost in training, although the latter exists to enhance it. Parsons values pulsebeats of unconscious life and shows how it is possible, even necessary, to evolve through complex relationships to unconscious processes. If one fails to find ways to work with unconscious being creatively, one pays a destructive price.

Psychoanalysis and psychotherapy do not exist in a vacuum: they are only a small part of a very long history of human beings trying to make sense of themselves and the world, which includes history, philosophy, science, religion and culture, among many other things. Mostly, however, we choose to see ourselves as small, precious objects floating in a rather hostile

universe. Both of these books in different ways put psychoanalysis in context, showing the struggle that has been taking place since Freud to understand where and how our work fits in - or doesn't - with the other ways in which we try to understand ourselves.

Both books are part of a series created by the Psychoanalysis Unit of University College London and the Anna Freud Centre. … [to] plead for recognition of the various forms of psychoanalytic research, but particularly to recognize their interrelatedness and even interdependence. Pauline Dalal  

This is a timely and welcome contribution to the field of psychoanalytic psychotherapy in general and to the sensitive area of cross-cultural work in particular. From its first line, ‘Slavery was a catastrophe for Africans and for Africa’ (p. 7), I was precipitated into an absorbing and compelling journey. Fletchman Smith's aim is two-pronged. One is to show how the trauma of slavery has left its mark on subsequent generations of Afro-Caribbean people in a variety of ways that need to be understood within the larger historical, social and cultural context. For this reason alone, the book was worth reading because it offers much that is relevant in thinking about our current social and political interrelations within the United Kingdom. Her interest, however, is in the way that individuals will find their own particular interpretations of, struggles within and solutions to the trauma - which leads to the other focus of the book: her assertion of the value of psychoanalytic ideas as a way of understanding people from this particular group who have psychological problems. She emphasizes the importance of a flexible attitude to theory and practice in order to avoid a further tyranny of fundamentalism.

This dual focus determines the shape of the book. In Part One, her first chapter gives a brief outline of the history of slavery and its legacy. It is not a simplified account of ‘goodies and baddies’. It does describe European and Arab exploitation but also points to practices by Africans themselves which contributed - for example, their own custom of taking slaves from other African states and their complicity in the selling of slaves. Nor does she pull punches. She is clear that ‘Britain was the chief European country involved in the organization of the slave trade’ (p. 18). Colonial and industrial expansion was founded on slavery. In this way, I think it is also a courageous book, confronting some difficult facts.

The impact and outcomes of slavery were obviously profound for all concerned. Slaves were not only physically removed from their families, countries, the food and climates they were used to, but were further alienated by being forbidden to speak their own languages. Later, when emancipation and independence were political realities, the struggle for equality as human beings at a psychological level was by no means achieved for these early losses had become deeply embedded states of mind - internalized object relations spanning generations. Some further legacies of this were not only the distortion of relationships and power between white and black, but within the Afro-Caribbean community itself. Fletchman Smith emphasizes the deleterious effects on the relations between Afro-Caribbean men and women, and, in particular, a ‘deep-rooted mistrust of women’ (p. 9). According to her, the men especially (and inevitably the internal world aspects of the male) have been most severely affected by the trauma of slavery.

Allan Schore  

It is an honor to be invited to present the Seventh Annual John Bowlby Memorial Lecture. Indeed, this is a double privilege in that it follows another last year, in which I was asked to write the Foreword to the re-issue of Bowlby's ground-breaking volume, Attachment (Bowlby 1969). In that work I surveyed, from a perspective at the close of what has been called ‘the decade of the brain’, his far-sighted proposals about the biological and neurological nature of attachment. Indeed, in a number of contributions I am describing how a spectrum of psychological and biological disciplines have adopted his ideas as the dominant model of human development available to science.

Each of these fields of scientific inquiry, when documenting the origins of the theory, points to Bowlby's integration of ethology (the study of behavioral biology) and psychoanalysis. In a contemporary description of the volume, Ainsworth wrote, ‘In effect what Bowlby has attempted is to update psychoanalytic theory in the light of recent advances in biology’ (Ainsworth 1969, p. 998). I suggest that in the three decades since the publication of Attachment, although the connections between attachment theory and science have deepened, those between itself and psychoanalysis, especially clinical psychoanalysis, have not. This situation is currently improving, however, due to the contributions of developmental psychoanalytic and psychological attachment research that demonstrate the clinical relevance of the concepts of mental representations of internal working models and reflective functions. Experimental and clinical attachment researchers are now describing, in detail, these two fundamental characteristics of ‘minds in the making’, the theme of this meeting.

It has sometimes been forgotten that attachment theory is a direct outgrowth of Freud's developmental perspective, not just a repudiation of some of his early speculations. Indeed, in the very first paragraph of Attachment Bowlby (1969) begins his ground-breaking work with specific reference to Freud's fundamental goal of understanding early development.

Mary Adams  

In one of the papers in the first issue of this impressive new journal, Psychoanalysis and History, the author says, ‘psychoanalysts have a very weak sense of their own history’ (Homans, 1(1): 70). I do not know how much this is true, but it raises interesting questions about the value of having a strong sense of our history for those of us in the analytic community and, further, which aspects of that history might be particularly important for us to absorb and think about.

Given the fact that, as practitioners, an important part of our work with patients aims towards establishing a greater sense of the generational boundaries, i.e. working through the Oedipus complex, it would seem essential that we ourselves have a firm sense of our own place in relation to our analytic family and the history of the psychoanalytic movement. Now, perhaps more than ever, with the dissolution in contemporary society of the extended family and traditional hierarchical structures, this is a particularly challenging aspect of our analytic work. For example, how do we address, with conviction, the narcissism in our patients and the perverse denial of difference, particularly generational difference (Chasseguet-Smirgel 1985) or denials of the ‘facts of life’ (Money-Kyrle 1971), unless we have a passionate sense and respect for the history and the personalities of our forebears.

What this new journal gives us in the first two issues is a lively feel for the history of psychoanalysis and the nature and humanity of the struggles faced by the people involved. And while any of the papers included would belong equally well in our already established psychoanalytic journals, developing a journal aimed specifically at giving us more of a sense of our own history does lend a special importance to the cultural roots of the psychoanalytic movement.

I was delighted that my paper in the BJP (Gerrard 2000) provoked such interest but I must admit I somewhat reeled from the ferocity of Martin Stanton's attack on my understanding of Balint. I had not set out, as he does so cogently, to give the reader an understanding of The Basic Fault and, as he rightly says, I did extract Balint's thoughts about interpretation of the transference to write a clinical paper of my own. However, it is rather disturbing that he feels I have ‘distorted’ Balint's theory.

As Balint writes, the basic fault is

a two-person relationship in which, however, only one of the partners matters; his wishes and needs are the only ones that count and must be attended to; the other partner, though felt to be immensely powerful, matters only in so far as he is willing to gratify the first partner's needs and desires or decides to frustrate them…. (Balint 1968, p. 23)

This led me to the clinical vignette quoted in full in the paper (Gerrard 2000, pp. 401-2). It is Balint's illustration of the above, but nevertheless the thoughts I offered about it are not negated by Balint's description of the patient in the area of the basic fault. Indeed Balint's response to his patient was an interpretation of the transference operating at the time between them, and indeed serves ‘to highlight the separateness and otherness of the analyst and/or patient’ (Stanton 2001, p. 546). The original state of harmony with one's environment having been disturbed by the discovery of separate objects, Balint posits, leads to the ocnophilic or philobatic response to try to recreate the original harmony. Stephen A. Mitchell 23 July 1946-21 December 2000

Bernice Laschinger and Kate White

Kate White

Kate White  

It is an immense honour to have been asked by the journal to write this obituary. The shock and sense of loss amongst the psychoanalytic community who knew Stephen Mitchell and his work, both here and, more particularly, in the United States, have been deeply felt. This we understand to be a reflection of the power, clarity and extraordinary humanity of his work which placed at its heart the mutually influencing relationship between analyst and analysand.

He was the leading member of a group of contemporary psychoanalysts identifying and shaping what has become known as the relational tradition in psychoanalysis. In the words of his colleagues from the journal he founded, Psychoanalytic Dialogues (Altmann & Messler Davies 2001):

His creative vision altered and expanded the landscape of psychoanalysis, infused it with energy and vitality, and changed the way we think, not only in psychoanalysis but also in related disciplines.

He was a training and supervising analyst at the William Alanson White Institute and supervisor and faculty member of the New York University Post Doctoral Programme in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis. His many publications include Hope and Dread in Psychoanalysis (1993), Freud and Beyond (1995, with Margaret Black), and Influence and Autonomy in Psychoanalysis (1997).

One of Stephen Mitchell's most significant early contributions lay in the brilliant challenges which he made to the self-referential defences of a psychoanalysis which viewed itself as largely independent of its social, cultural and political context. Mitchell's contention was that theories do not exist in isolation: they belong to a particular time and place and exist and gain meaning in dialogue with each other. Just as we have no existence as people in isolation, we emerge from a matrix of relationships (without which the whole notion of individuation cannot have any meaning), so too with theories: they also emerge from a matrix of historical and cultural relationships from which they gain meaning.

In the therapist's prefatory remarks to the clinical material the therapist comments that she is not reporting whole sessions but only selected ‘elements’. The reader's attention is drawn to the fact that this is not the full

picture and that there are gaps or missing pieces. The effect of this, in conjunction with the partial or fragmentary selection of material, is frustrating and tantalizing. The editor in her introduction draws attention to a similar feature when she comments on the ‘unadorned’ style of the written word. In the account of the first assessment session the therapist twice comments on the patient not being ‘forthcoming’. There is a similar effect between patient and therapist to that between writer and reader, and we might wonder if something of significance is being reproduced or replicated.

During the first meeting of therapist and patient, the therapist finds herself ‘wondering what moved him emotionally’ and towards the end of this first meeting, though Gregg has told her a number of ‘facts’ about himself, she has ‘no idea what he felt about anything’. It is when she tells him this that there seems to be more of an emotional connection between them - Gregg ‘was really taken with this’ and the therapist's comment leads to mutual recognition and a ‘sense of relief’. Other countertransference experiences which the therapist describes, in subsequent sessions, include feeling ‘cut off’, the ‘painful’ silence, and being ‘sent… into a spin’. This is a significant book. Understanding the Trauma of Racial Violence in a Black Patient

Narendra Keval

Narendra Keval

36 Ashurst Close, Northwood, Middlesex HA6 1EL. [email: narendra.keval@talk21.com]

Narendra Keval  

Racial violence arises when infantile anxiety and hatred of ‘difference’ or ‘otherness’ become too unmanageable within the self and are displaced into the racial arena via splitting and projective mechanisms. The body of the ‘other’, particularly skin colour differences, becomes a salient target for locating and attacking these feared and unwanted aspects of the self.

Those on the receiving end can experience a profound attack on their identity, with feelings of rejection that can result in a severe narcissistic blow, puncturing and even shattering the individual's psychic skin and existing defensive organization. This failure of containment can send tremors throughout the psyche to some of the most vulnerable areas in individuals functioning, giving fresh life to both oedipal and pre-oedipal anxieties to do with separation and loss.

Where these early anxieties are felt to be unbearable, the individual resorts to encapsulating them in a portion of their mind, effectively sealing them off from conscious awareness or access, but they are unconsciously re-enacted. A case study aims to describe some of these phenomena.

Brendan McLoughlin

Brendan McLoughlin

Bath

Brendan McLoughlin  

In this slim volume Jacobs undertakes a comparatively large task, the elaboration of a psychodynamic interpretation of thinking and belief. In his opening chapter he states:

This book is about belief, but it is not confined to religion. It is about the way people believe … It is also about knowledge … about the way people know, or think they know, or even believe they know. (p. 1)

It is a book which has grown and developed from its first presentation in 1987, through a second version in 1993 to this most recent incarnation. This progress perhaps reflects Jabobs's own journey from the theological paradigm to the psychoanalytic and in some ways it represents a work of repair and redemption as much of the psychoanalytic viewpoint as of the religious perspective.

Jacobs takes Freud's concept of religion as an illusion and expands it to include all thinking, knowing and believing. In doing this he builds on Winnicott's thinking on illusion (Winnicott 1975, p. 239): ‘The mother's adaptation to the infant's needs, when good enough, gives the infant the illusion that there is an external reality that corresponds to the infant's own capacity to create.’ The work of Winnicott and Bion inform Jacobs's fundamental view of illusion as being of crucial significance in development, in culture and religion, and in the psychodynamics of knowing and believing. Much of the opening chapter, ‘Illusions of knowledge and belief’, is spent in constructing the argument that illusion is a necessary and purposeful element in ordinary human experience, right from infancy and into adult life. Jacobs is careful to point out that he is not concerned with the content of illusion, whether it be right or wrong, so much as with its purpose in normal psychological functioning.

Regression, Dependency and the Evolution of the Self

Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine

56 Osbaldeston Road, London N16 7DR. [email: margvalentine@hotmail.com]

Marguerite Valentine  

This paper is about the difficulties in working with the regressed or borderline patient. Drawing on clinical material, and recent empirical research on mother-infant interaction, theoretical explanations are considered. It is noted that these theories contain, by implication, guidance for psychotherapeutic practice. For patients functioning at this level of emotional development, techniques of traditional psychoanalysis are eschewed in favour of a ‘relational’ model, which draws on the therapist's capacity to be empathically engaged with the patient's internal and external world. Working in this way, it is argued, regressive periods can be seen as containing a potential for the patient's evolution of self.

Clinical Material

Simona Crean

Simona Crean

15 Landrock Road, London N8 9HR

Simona Crean  

Gregg was referred to me recently by a psychotherapy training organization. It is the early stages of the work. I saw him for two assessment sessions (which is my usual practice) in March. There was then a two-week Easter break. I have seen him for nine sessions to date. He comes once a week. I will report the assessment sessions and the first two sessions fairly fully and then aspects of further sessions. I have chosen to present only elements from the sessions that seem interesting, engaging or puzzling.

Assessment Session 1

Gregg arrived five minutes early. I did not ask him to wait. I noticed he was not wearing a watch and wondered about timekeeping. I thought he looked rather attractive in a rakish way. I guessed he was in his 30s. He was wearing jeans and carrying a rucksack.

I asked him to tell me something about himself and he said that he was 36, his wife was from a northern European country, and that he had two young children. He has two sisters, both younger than himself.

I asked him about his previous therapy, which he had mentioned when he rang asking for his first appointment. He had seen a male psychotherapist in central London via a friend. The friend also saw the same psychotherapist. When I asked why he had not continued he said he had seen him twice but found the journey too much. He told me that he had some counselling when he was going to be married and his wife-to-be was about to come to England. He thought he should do something about his behaviour. He went to his GP and saw the surgery counsellor for six sessions. He did not feel this did any good.

Ilana Laor  

By identifying the three fundamentals of brief psychoanalytic psychotherapy - (1) time limit, (2) therapeutic focus, (3) therapist's activity - this type of therapy is established as a distinct therapeutic modality with distinct ‘active containing’. The way this ‘custom-tailored structure’ may be adapted to the patient and used to reflect and intensify dynamic aspects of the treatment's focus is demonstrated through clinical material.

Mad Men and Medusa: Reclaiming Hysteria and the Effects of Sibling Relations on the Human Condition by Juliet Mitchell. Published by Allen Lane, Penguin Press, London, 2000; 381 pages; £20.00.

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

London

Prophecy Coles  

This is a complex book for, as Mitchell says, ‘This book should be read as a verbal picture rather than a narrative. Its structure is like a dandelion flower, a compositae in which each floret is an independent unit but each is needed to make a connected whole’ (p. 42). I will return later to the difficulty that this structure places upon the reader.

There are two interrelated arguments that weave through this richly documented book. The first argument puts forward the idea that psychoanalytic theory has neglected our lateral relationships with our siblings and peers. The second argument claims that psychoanalytic theory has turned its back upon hysteria. These two ideas fit together in the following way. Mitchell believes that hysteria has not disappeared, though its features have been obscured by the failure to recognize its precipitating causes. Hysteria is the anguished response of the infant who feels displaced and dispossessed by the birth of a sibling. The birth of a sibling overthrows the certainty of things, and one's place in the world is no longer felt to be secure. Suddenly the elder child finds his position is threatened by someone who stands essentially in the same relationship to the parents. This can be a ‘catastrophe’ (p. 331) and an experience of fragmentation can take place. ‘Where am I?’ (p. 319) is the theme of this childish nightmare. The result of this experience is to push the displaced child into a regressive position, in the hope of gaining the mother's attention and love again. However, this regressive position is overlaid with other developmental experiences. The elder child will have begun to have sexual fantasies and will be aware of absences and endings and have some concept of death. Therefore this regressive pull will be complicated with fantasies of sex and violence attached to it. Murder will be ‘in the air’ (p. 20) as the elder child wishes to murder the intruder. This is the basis of hysteria and we all wish to repudiate it, for it frightens us. Hysteria involves violence, evil and cruelty. Intricate games of hide and seek with the dominant ideology are played by the hysteric, in an effort not to be known. The hysteric gets under one's skin. The hysteric suffers somatic symptoms that have no organic basis, such as mutism, fainting and breathing difficulties. In other words, the hysteric causes a lot of trouble. At the core of hysteria is a fantasy that Mitchell calls the ‘parthenogenic complex’ (p. xi). This fantasy embodies the belief that babies can be produced without intercourse. It is an infantile and omnipotent fantasy that repudiates the need for the other. Another, and seemingly paradoxical, component to this fantasy can be the belief that one has been seduced.

Jan RøVik

Jan RøVik

Postbox 3084 Elisenberg, 0207 Oslo, Norway. [email: jan.ole.roevik@enitel.no]

Jan RøVik  

Two patients, one with an overt and the other with a covert narcissistic disorder, are followed through five years of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. A number of important turning points in the therapies are closely evaluated in order to discover possible mutative elements. Special attention is paid to the patients' self-sufficiency. The attachment process to the therapist and the patients' gradual acceptance of healthy dependency are described. The theoretical framework is selfpsychological.

Transference, Countertransference, Society and Culture: Before and during the First Encounter

Antonio Suman and Antonino Brignone

Antonino Brignone

Via Bandi 5, 50137 Firenze, Italy

Antonino Brignone  

Our contribution focuses on the first encounter with the patient and on the social and cultural context in which it takes place; we believe that psychotherapy begins with the very first encounter, whether or not it leads to a therapeutic relationship. Before the first encounter, the patient produces conscious and unconscious fantasies, sometimes even dreams, about the therapy, the therapist and the encounter itself; these fantasies constitute a sort of preformed, cultural transference. Besides the preformed transference, an actual transference relationship begins to develop, becoming activated in the patient by contact with the real person of the therapist, and in the therapist by contact with the real person of the patient, blending with the culturally preformed transference. This primitive transference can rapidly determine the outcome of the first encounter as well as of the actual project of entering therapy.
